payload.rationale: Historically, measles cases in the United States have remained relatively low since the disease was declared eliminated in 2000, largely due to high baseline vaccination coverage. The largest recent outbreak occurred in 2019 with 1,282 cases, which was the highest number since 1992. A threshold of over 6,000 cases in a single year (2026) would represent an unprecedented, massive outbreak nearly five times larger than the 2019 peak. While vaccine hesitancy and localized outbreaks remain a concern, a nationwide failure of herd immunity sufficient to produce 6,000 cases in one year is highly improbable. The strongest reason this estimate could be too high is that the base rate for such an event is practically zero in the modern era, making even a 1% chance generous. The strongest reason it could be too low is if anti-vaccine sentiment or disruptions to routine pediatric immunizations escalated dramatically between the present and 2026, leading to a sudden, widespread epidemic.
limitations: No current data or CDC statistics for 2026 were provided.
Forecast relies entirely on historical base rates and general background knowledge.
